value.overview: The Black-striped Sparrow (Arremonops conirostris) is a medium-sized New World sparrow of humid tropical regions from Honduras through northern South America. It is usually found in dense shrubs, forest edges, young second growth, and other tangled vegetation rather than deep forest. The species often stays low and partly hidden while searching the ground for food. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident, especially in humid lowlands and foothill habitats on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes.
value.classification: The Black-striped Sparrow belongs to the family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows, and the genus Arremonops. Its scientific name is Arremonops conirostris.
value.identification: This chunky sparrow is about 16.5 cm long. Adults have a gray head marked by strong black stripes along the crown and through the eye, an olive-green to olive-brown back, and mostly pale grayish or whitish underparts with olive or brown tones on the flanks. The bill is dark, sometimes with a paler or yellowish base, and the eyes are reddish brown. Males and females look alike. Juveniles are duller, with more yellowish-olive and brown tones and less sharply defined head markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from eastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, with additional populations in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Brazil, and nearby regions. In Costa Rica it is a common resident of the lower foothills and humid lowlands throughout the Caribbean slope and in the southern Pacific region, extending north on the Pacific side to the Carara area. It is scarce or absent in the dry northwestern lowlands. It uses humid scrub, weedy fields, young second growth, shaded plantations, gardens, forest borders, and dense streamside vegetation, usually from the lowlands to about 1,500 m.
value.migrationStatus: The Black-striped Sparrow is generally resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Some local or seasonal movements may occur, especially at higher elevations, where it can be a seasonal breeding resident.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from February through July, with as many as two broods in a season. The bulky domed nest is made from coarse plant material and usually placed in dense vegetation only 15 to 90 cm above the ground; nests are occasionally on the ground or higher. The nest has a broad side entrance. A clutch usually contains two immaculate white eggs, with three reported less often.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-striped Sparrow feeds mainly on the ground or very close to it. Its diet includes seeds and other plant matter, along with insects and other small invertebrates; fruits and berries may also be taken. It commonly scratches through leaf litter and probes among low vegetation, especially along forest edges, in thickets, gardens, and second-growth habitats. Dense cover allows it to forage while remaining difficult to see.
value.behavior: This species is usually encountered alone, in pairs, or in family groups, and it does not normally form large flocks. It moves deliberately through shrubs, vines, and leaf litter, often keeping low and remaining partly concealed. Its voice is an important clue to its presence, as it gives a distinctive, musical song and call notes from dense cover. During the breeding season, pairs defend territories around suitable nesting vegetation.
